blockers.quote: Stanley Milgram, 1963. 40 men, a panel of switches, a stranger in the next room taking the shocks. 26 of them went all the way to the last switch. 450 volts. (c06)
blockers.why: Claim c06. Stating that a stranger in the next room was 'taking the shocks' is factually false: the learner was an actor/confederate and no actual shocks were administered or taken. While participants believed shocks were delivered, asserting as real-world fact that someone was 'taking the shocks' misstates the experiment. Furthermore, the c06 ledger note explicitly directs: 'Say "published in 1963"; if a run year is said, "1961", never a month.' Saying 'Stanley Milgram, 1963' misleads on the study's run date (conducted in 1961 at Yale).
blockers.fix: Stanley Milgram, published in 1963. 40 men, a panel of switches, a stranger in the next room they believed was taking the shocks. 26 of them went all the way to the last switch. 450 volts. (c06)

blockers.quote: In the real study, at a real photocopier, an empty reason worked about as well as a real one, for a small favour. Nobody was being kind. Nobody was listening. (c03)
blockers.why: Claim c03. The claim that 'Nobody was being kind. Nobody was listening' is unsupported and contradicts Langer et al. (1978). In that study, 60% of people agreed to let someone cut in with no reason at all, demonstrating baseline kindness/helpfulness. The finding was mindless compliance with the syntactic structure of a request ('because...'), not that people were unkind or deaf to the ask. The verbatim quote supports only the placebic request wording.
blockers.fix: In the real study, at a real photocopier, an empty reason worked about as well as a real one, for a small favour. (c03)
